lead: Before choosing a bus, an engineer asks four questions: how are the nodes wired together (topology), who is allowed to start a message (network organization), how is a clash on the wire avoided (control mechanism), and how fast and how safe must it be (class). The OSI reference model gives a common language for the answers, because it splits communication into seven layers and lets us say exactly which jobs a bus such as CAN does and which it leaves to software. This chapter gives the topologies, the access methods, the seven layers and the bus classes, with the numbers an examiner asks for.
prereq: You need vehicle networking and the need for data buses: nodes, messages, bus load and the requirements for a bus.

blocks.text: Topology is the shape of the wiring between nodes. Five shapes appear in cars:

head: Topology
How it is wired
Effect of one broken cable
Vehicle example
rows: One trunk cable; each node taps it with a short stub
A trunk break splits the bus and removes a terminator, so usually the whole bus fails; a stub break loses one node
Every node has its own cable to a central hub or switch
Only that node is lost; the centre is a single point of failure
Automotive Ethernet switch, FlexRay active star
Each node is wired to the next and the last back to the first
A single ring stops completely; a double ring survives
Nodes in a row, each passing data to the next
Nodes beyond the break are lost
Buses and stars joined, often through gateways
Depends on where the break is

blocks.text: A bus needs the least cable and is easy to extend; a star needs the most but isolates faults; a ring suits a continuous stream such as audio but needs every node working.

Network organization says who may start a transfer. In master-slave organization one master starts every exchange and the slaves only answer (LIN). In multi-master organization any node may start (CAN). Software then follows a client-server pattern (a tester asks, an ECU answers) or a producer-consumer pattern (a node broadcasts a value and every interested node takes it).

Addressing says how a receiver knows a message is for it. Subscriber-oriented addressing puts the address of the receiving node in the message. Message-oriented addressing gives the content a number (CAN's identifier means "engine speed", not "for the cluster"), and each node filters the numbers it wants. Transmission-oriented addressing identifies a message by its time slot (FlexRay's static segment).
The control mechanism, or bus access method, decides who may use the shared wire at a given moment:

items: Centralised, deterministic: master-slave polling. The master's schedule fixes every slot, so latency is known (LIN).
Decentralised, deterministic: time-division multiple access (TDMA), where each node owns fixed time slots (FlexRay static segment), or token passing, where only the node holding the token may send.

Random access: carrier sense multiple access (CSMA). A node sends when the bus is idle. In CSMA/CD (collision detection, early office Ethernet) a collision destroys both frames and both retry. In CAN's version, often called CSMA/CR (collision resolution), the clash is settled bit by bit so the higher-priority frame survives undamaged.

blocks.text: The OSI (Open Systems Interconnection) reference model splits communication into seven layers. Each layer uses the service of the one below.

head: Layer
Job
In a CAN network
In automotive Ethernet
rows: Meaning of the data, services for programs
Splitting long data into packets and rebuilding it
Framing, access to the medium, error checks
Voltage levels, bit timing, cable, connector

blocks.text: CAN defines only layers 1 and 2; layers 3 to 6 are mostly empty, because control messages are short and stay inside the car. When a message is longer than one frame (a diagnostic reply, a software download), a transport protocol at layer 4 cuts it into numbered pieces. In ISO-TP on classic CAN, a single frame carries up to 7 data bytes; a longer message starts with a first frame carrying 6 data bytes and continues with consecutive frames of 7 data bytes each, after the receiver has sent one flow control frame.
SAE sorts vehicle networks into classes by data rate and the job they do. Many textbooks add a higher class for the newer fast buses.

head: Class
Data rate
Typical use
Example buses
rows: Body: switches, mirrors, window lifters, seat motors
Body and comfort data shared between ECUs, instrument cluster
Above 1 Mbit/s (often called C+ or D)
X-by-wire and safety (C+); multimedia and cameras (D)
FlexRay, CAN FD, MOST, automotive Ethernet

blocks.text: Buses are also classed by application: diagnostic, safety (airbag sensors), multimedia and x-by-wire.

examples.question: A scan tool asks for the vehicle identification number (VIN). The engine ECU's reply is 20 bytes long: 3 bytes of service and record number, then the 17 VIN characters. It travels on classic CAN using ISO-TP. How many CAN frames does the ECU send, and how many bytes does each carry? Which OSI layers are at work?
steps: A single frame holds at most 7 data bytes; 20 > 7, so the reply must be segmented.
First frame: it carries the total length (20) in its header and the first 6 data bytes. Bytes left: 20 − 6 = 14.
The scan tool answers with one flow control frame that says "send the rest".
Consecutive frame 1 carries 7 bytes: 14 − 7 = 7 left. Consecutive frame 2 carries the last 7 bytes: 7 − 7 = 0 left.
ECU frames: 1 first frame + 2 consecutive frames = 3 frames, carrying 6 + 7 + 7 = 20 bytes.

Layers: the VIN request and reply are layer 7 (an OBD service); the cutting into first and consecutive frames is layer 4; each frame's arbitration and CRC are layer 2; the voltages on the twisted pair are layer 1.
examples.answer: The ECU sends 3 frames (6 + 7 + 7 data bytes) after the tester's flow control frame; layers 7, 4, 2 and 1 are used, and layers 3, 5 and 6 are empty.

examples.question: Find the raw data rate each function needs and name its bus class. (a) A door module sends 8 frames of 100 bits every 100 ms. (b) The engine and gearbox exchange 30 messages of 125 bits every 20 ms. (c) A rear camera sends 640 × 480 pixels at 16 bits per pixel, 30 pictures per second, uncompressed.
steps: (a) 8 × 100 bits ÷ 0.100 s = 800 ÷ 0.100 = 8000 bit/s = 8 kbit/s. Below 10 kbit/s: Class A; a 19.2 kbit/s LIN bus is 42 per cent loaded (8 ÷ 19.2 = 0.417).
(b) 30 × 125 bits ÷ 0.020 s = 3750 ÷ 0.020 = 187 500 bit/s = 187.5 kbit/s. Between 125 kbit/s and 1 Mbit/s: Class C; a 500 kbit/s CAN bus is 37.5 per cent loaded.
This is above 100 Mbit/s, so 100BASE-T1 cannot carry it uncompressed; it needs a multimedia-class link such as 1000BASE-T1 Ethernet, or compression.
examples.answer: (a) 8 kbit/s, Class A (LIN). (b) 187.5 kbit/s, Class C (500 kbit/s CAN). (c) 147.5 Mbit/s, the multimedia class above 1 Mbit/s (gigabit Ethernet or compressed video).

traps: CAN is not a seven-layer stack. The CAN standard covers layers 1 and 2 only; transport (ISO-TP) and application (UDS, OBD) are separate standards.
Master-slave is an organization, not a topology. LIN is master-slave on a bus topology; a star is a wiring shape.
CAN does not use CSMA/CD. In CSMA/CD a collision destroys both frames; in CAN the higher-priority frame wins the clash without damage.
SAE defines Classes A, B and C. Name C+ or D as a textbook extension for buses above 1 Mbit/s, and say which buses you mean.
A single ring is not fault tolerant: one broken fibre in a MOST ring stops the whole ring.

quiz.q: Name the seven OSI layers from the bottom up.
quiz.a: Physical, data link, network, transport, session, presentation, application.

quiz.q: Give the data-rate band of SAE Class A, B and C networks with one bus for each.
quiz.a: A: below 10 kbit/s, LIN. B: 10 to 125 kbit/s, low-speed CAN. C: 125 kbit/s to 1 Mbit/s, high-speed CAN.

quiz.q: Explain message-oriented addressing with CAN as the example.
quiz.a: The identifier names the content (for example engine speed), not the receiver. Every node receives every frame and its filter keeps only the identifiers it needs, so a new receiver can be added without changing the sender.

quiz.q: Why are OSI layers 3 to 6 mostly empty in an in-vehicle CAN network?
quiz.a: Control messages are short, fit in one frame and stay inside the car, so no routing, session or format layers are needed. Only long diagnostic data uses a transport layer (ISO-TP).

quiz.q: A diagnostic reply of 34 bytes travels by ISO-TP on classic CAN. How many frames does the ECU send?
quiz.a: First frame 6 bytes, leaving 28. 28 ÷ 7 = 4 consecutive frames. Total 1 + 4 = 5 frames (6 + 4 × 7 = 34 bytes).

quiz.q: Compare bus, star and ring topologies for a body network of 12 door, seat and lamp modules.
quiz.a: A bus uses the least cable and is easy to extend, but a trunk break can stop it. A star isolates each module but needs 12 cables to a hub, too costly for slow modules. A ring stops completely on one break. A bus (CAN plus LIN sub-buses) is the usual choice for cost.

beyond: Not for the exam. Vehicle networks are moving toward the full IP stack: diagnostics over IP (DoIP) and SOME/IP use layers 3 and 4, and time-sensitive networking adds deterministic scheduling to Ethernet. Search for DoIP, SOME/IP and the AUTOSAR communication stack.
